# Implement block: Tangram Snap (Jetpack Compose)

You are adding the "Tangram Snap" block from Native Cook to the user's Android app. The block already exists as working Kotlin code. Your job is to bring it into this project faithfully, not to write a new one that looks similar.

## The block

A tangram on a dark lacquered board: the seven classic pieces in exact proportion (two large triangles, a medium and two small ones, a square and a parallelogram) in vermilion, indigo, ochre, jade, plum, teal and cream lacquer over wood grain, with bevelled edges, a gloss across their upper left and soft shadows. The faint outline of a figure fills the top of the screen and the loose pieces wait in a felt-lined well below it. Small capitals read "Tangram · No. 1 of 4" over the figure's name in a serif ("The Cat") and the hint "Drag · Tap to turn · Double-tap to flip", with a live count ("3 / 7", "In place") at the top right; four small silhouettes along the bottom (a cat, a sailing boat, a runner, a swan) choose the figure, the current one in its own colour. When the last piece goes in, the figure becomes one solid shape in its colour and the line reads "Seven pieces, one shape." Everything is drawn: no photos.

**Motion.** One clock drives everything: ticks of 1/60 s, at most three a frame. A piece lifts as soon as it is touched (on a spring of 380/s² and 36/s, growing 5% while its shadow moves 8 pt right and 13 pt down and softens) and follows the finger on a stiff spring (900/s², 52/s). Within 64 pt of a free slot of its kind at a matching turn (within 0.3 rad) it is drawn towards the slot, up to 70% of the way, and the slot glows in its colour. Let go within 34 pt of such a slot (at the release point or 0.09 s of its speed further on), it snaps in on a magnetic spring with a little overshoot (420/s², 24/s), a ring of light spreads from the slot over 0.6 s and a light haptic ticks; otherwise the finger's speed carries it on a free spring (210/s², 26/s) to where it settles, rounded to the nearest 45°. A tap turns a piece 45° clockwise and two fingers turn it freely (both on a spring of 260/s² and 28/s, snapping to 45° on release); a double tap flips it face down through a horizontal squeeze (180/s², 26.8/s); each with a selection haptic, and each checks whether the piece now fits where it lies. When all seven are in, a success haptic plays and over 1.1 s the colour floods out from the last piece in a widening circle while every piece fades to the figure's colour, its bevels and the hairline gaps between pieces close and the outline fades, until the figure is one solid lacquered shape with a soft shadow and sheen. Choosing another figure morphs the outline into it over 1.2 s on an ease-in-out curve, each slot moving and turning to its place in the new figure while the loose pieces fly home one after another 0.06 s apart, lifted for 0.28 s; a solved figure instead carries its pieces into the new figure as one solid shape, holds for 1.1 s, then comes apart. The self-playing demo loops every 13 s: from the empty cat, it sets the pieces one by one every 0.74 s from 0.8 s, each lifted along an arc over 0.58 s while it turns and flips into place; the cat fills by 7.2 s, turns into the swan with its pieces at 7.9 s, holds, and at 10.3 s comes apart as the outline morphs back to the cat, resting until the loop starts over from exactly the same state. A touch stops it for 5 s, after which it takes the figure apart and starts again. Under reduced motion the demo does not play, snaps settle without overshoot, two-finger turns step in 45° increments, a release does not glide, and morphs take 0.3 s.

## Reference source

The block is built and running in the Native Cook source repository. Each link below is a file on GitHub. To read one as plain text, replace `https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/` with `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/` in its address.

### Demo (start here)

- [TangramSnapDemo.kt](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/kotlin/app/src/main/java/com/ngocdevv/nativecook/blocks/playground/tangramsnap/TangramSnapDemo.kt)

### Files of the block

- [TangramSnap.kt](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/kotlin/app/src/main/java/com/ngocdevv/nativecook/blocks/playground/tangramsnap/TangramSnap.kt)
- [TangramSnapEngine.kt](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/kotlin/app/src/main/java/com/ngocdevv/nativecook/blocks/playground/tangramsnap/TangramSnapEngine.kt)
- [TangramSnapModel.kt](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/kotlin/app/src/main/java/com/ngocdevv/nativecook/blocks/playground/tangramsnap/TangramSnapModel.kt)
- [TangramSnapPainter.kt](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/kotlin/app/src/main/java/com/ngocdevv/nativecook/blocks/playground/tangramsnap/TangramSnapPainter.kt)

### Libraries

## Your instructions

_Anything specific to this app goes here: where the block should appear, what to rename, what to change. Left empty, integrate the block as it is._

## How to work

Work like an experienced Android engineer joining an existing project: learn the app first, read only what you need, decide early how the block fits, then integrate it with as little disruption as possible. Take the steps in order.

**Done means** the block is reachable in the user's app and behaves like the reference on an emulator or a device. A Compose preview is useful while you work, but it is not the proof: build, install and run the app.

**Fidelity.** Bring over the real implementation. Keep its structure, colours, sizes, timings and easing. Change only what this project requires and what "Your instructions" ask for.

If you already learned this project earlier in the conversation, reuse what you know and skip step 2. Learn it again only if the project changed or something you need is missing.

### 1. Check where you are

- You need the project's files and a terminal. If this prompt was pasted into a chat that has neither, stop and say so: it has to be run by a coding agent opened on the project.
- Confirm the project is an Android app built with Gradle. If it is something else, stop, say what you found, and do not create a new app inside it unless the instructions ask for one.

### 2. Learn the host app

- The app module, its namespace, `minSdk`, `compileSdk`, and the versions of Kotlin, the Android Gradle Plugin and Compose (a BOM or single versions).
- Whether Compose is switched on in that module, and whether screens are Compose, Views or both.
- Navigation: Navigation Compose, fragments, activities, or a single screen. Find how a screen is added today.
- How dependencies are declared: a version catalog (`libs.versions.toml`) or directly in `build.gradle`.
- Conventions: package layout, naming, theme, where resources live and how they are named.

### 3. Read the block

- Open the demo, then each file in the block's package. The list above names every file of the block, and the resources it uses from outside its package.
- The demo is how the source repository shows the block. Bring over what the demo shows, not the repository's gallery. Anything listed under "Used by the demo only" stays behind.
- Read the block's parameters and their defaults. The demo may switch on an option that makes the block play by itself for a recording (for example `autoPlay`). Keep the option; leave it off in the user's app unless asked.

### 4. Decide the fit

- Compare the block's libraries and the versions it was built with to the host's. Add what is missing the way this project declares dependencies. Do not upgrade the host's Kotlin, Gradle plugin or Compose versions without asking; if an API differs on the host's version, adapt the block's code.
- Check `minSdk`. If the block uses an API newer than the host's minimum, keep the fallback the source has, or tell the user what would be lost.
- If Compose is not switched on in the module, say what turning it on involves before you do it. In a View-based screen, show the block through a `ComposeView`.
- Shared helpers: copy the ones the block imports next to it, or fold them into the block's files. Do not copy helpers it never calls.

### 5. Bring it in

- Copy the block's files into a package of this app, and rewrite the `package` lines and the imports, including the import of the app's own `R` class.
- Copy its resources and asset files. Keep their names unless one collides with a resource of the app; then rename it everywhere it is used.
- Keep reduced-motion handling, haptics and accessibility descriptions as they are in the source. If the block needs a permission, add it to the manifest and say so.
- Mount the block where the instructions say. With no instructions, add a screen or destination named after the block and make it reachable the way the app's other screens are.

### 6. Run it

- Build with the project's own task, for example `./gradlew :app:assembleDebug`, and fix every error and new warning the block introduced.
- Install and run it, and use the block: every state, every gesture, and once with animations switched off in the system settings.
- If the build or the emulator fails for a reason outside the block, report the error and ask how to continue.

### 7. Report

- Files added and changed, dependencies and permissions added, and anything renamed to avoid a collision.
- How to reach the block in the app.
- Anything that differs from the reference, and why.
